competition: Bangladesh Mathematical Olympiad, National Round (Higher Secondary)

problems.problem:
(a) Find the domain and range of the function $f(x)=\left|x^3+1\right|$ and sketch the graph. For which value of $x$ is the derivative of the function undefined? Find the inverse, if any, of the given function; if there is no inverse explain why not.

(b) Find the domain and range of the function $f(x)=x\left(x^2-1\right)$. Find the local maximum point and local minimum point of the function. Find the coordinates of the points of intersection of the curve with the axes, if any. Then sketch the curve. If there are any absolute maximum and absolute minimum points, find them.

Find the solution sets, if any, of the following equation and inequality:

(a) $|x-1|-|x|=2$

(b) $\left|\frac{3}{x}-2\right|\le 3$

Three circles each of radius $1$ m are such that they touch each other. In the space inside the circles a circle is drawn so that it touches the three circles.

(a) What is the radius of the circle drawn?

(b) Considering the centre of the drawn circle as the origin and the line joining the origin to the centre of any of the three circles as the $x$-axis of the Cartesian coordinate system, find the equations of all the circles.

The centre of an ellipse is at the origin, its major axis is along the $x$-axis and its minor axis along the $y$-axis; the major axis is of length $6$ and the eccentricity is $\sqrt{5}/3$.

(a) Write the equation of the ellipse.

(b) Find the areas of the three parts of the ellipse divided by the two latera recta.

(c) Find the area enclosed by the tangent to the ellipse at $\left(2,2\sqrt{5}/3\right)$, the segment of the ellipse in the first quadrant, the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis.

Two circles of radii $2$ m and $1$ m intersect at $A$ and $B$, where $AB=0.4$ m. A point $P$ is considered on the smaller circle equidistant from $A$ and $B$ so that the extensions of $PA$ and $PB$ intersect the bigger circle at $C$ and $D$ respectively. Find the length of the chord $CD$.

An inclined plane of length $40$ m is inclined to the horizontal at an angle $30^\circ$. From the foot of this plane a body starts from rest and moves up the plane with an acceleration $10\ \text{m/s}^2$. After moving a distance of $30$ m on the plane the acceleration is stopped. If it is supposed that the effect of gravity is always there, the resistance of the plane is zero and there is no resistance of air, then at what horizontal distance from the beginning of the journey will the body strike the ground?

On a vertical wall there is a point $A$ at which one end of a rope is attached; at another point $B$, which is vertically below $A$, one end of another rope is attached. The other ends of the ropes are knotted together at $C$. Now a force of $75$ N is applied at $C$ along $BC$ and a force of $60$ N is applied at $C$ in the vertically downward direction. If $AC$ and $BC$ are inclined to the vertical at angles $30^\circ$ and $60^\circ$ respectively, find the magnitudes of the tensions in the ropes.

A geometric series is given by
$$a\left(r+r^2+\cdots\right)=ar\frac{1}{1-r}\qquad\text{for } r<1.$$
Using the geometric series, express the number $0.\overline{021}$ as a fraction.

Suppose $A=\{0,2,4,6,\ldots,50\}$. Find
$$\sum_{S\in P(A)}\max(S),$$
where $P(A)$ is the set of all subsets of $A$ and $\max(S)$ is the largest element of $S$.

In the binomial expansion of
$$\left(3x^2+\frac{a}{x^3}\right)^{10}$$
the coefficients of $x^5$ and $x^{15}$ are found to be equal. Find $a$.
The roots of the equation $z^3+8=0$ form an equilateral triangle in the complex plane. Find the length of any side of this triangle.
A rectangle is to be inscribed in a semicircle of radius $2$. What is the largest area the rectangle can have?

(a) Find
$$\frac{d}{dx}\log\left(\sin\left(x^2+1\right)\right).$$

(b) Evaluate
$$\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{2}} x\sin^2\left(2x^2\right)dx.$$
Find a formula for Pythagorean triples ($a^2+b^2=c^2$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are integers) that are not necessarily multiples of one another.

Find all ordered pairs $(x,y)$ with $x>y$ such that
$$\begin{cases} x^2+xy+y^2=7\times 19\\ x+y+\sqrt{xy}=19\end{cases}$$
Distinct points $A$ and $B$ are on a semicircle with diameter $MN$ and center $C$. The point $P$ is on $CN$ and $\angle CBP=\angle CAP=20^\circ$. If $\angle MCA=50^\circ$, what is $\angle BCP$?

Solve the inequality
$$\frac{3x\left(x^2-5x+6\right)}{(x-2)(x+3)}\ge 0.$$

(i) If $n$ is a composite integer, then $n$ has a prime divisor less than or equal to $\sqrt{n}$; using this statement prove that $2087$ is prime.

(ii) How many integer solutions does
$$xy+9(x+y)=2006$$
have?
For each integer $n\ge 2$ determine, with proof, which of the two positive real numbers $a$, $b$ satisfying $a^n=a+1$, $b^{2n}=b+3a$ is larger.

Find the sum
$$S=\frac{F_0}{6^0}+\frac{F_1}{6^1}+\frac{F_2}{6^2}+\frac{F_3}{6^3}+\frac{F_4}{6^4}+\cdots$$
where $F_0=1$, $F_1=1$ and $F_n=F_{n-1}+F_{n-2}$ for $n\ge 2$.
Suppose we want to make a pyramid with a square base out of stone balls. If we need $n$ stone balls for a base line, then how many stone balls of the same size do we need to make the pyramid?

Find the formula $A(a)$ for the area of the region bounded by the lines $x=0$, $y=0$, $x=a$ (where $0\le a\le 8$) and the function
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}3, & \text{if } 0\le x\le 3\\ e^x, & \text{if } x>3\end{cases}$$
Hence find $A(3)$ and $A(8)$.

(i) Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ where $y=\dfrac{x^{\frac{1}{2}\sqrt[4]{7x-14}}}{\left(1-x^3\right)^3}$.

(ii) Evaluate $\int_0^{\frac{\pi}{4}} x^2\cos^2 2x\,dx$.
Find the last two (rightmost) digits of $3^{999}$.

Suppose food of type $A$ of price $40$ Tk. has $8$ units of protein and $10$ units of starch. Another food of type $B$ of price $50$ Tk. has $12$ units of protein and $6$ units of starch. If we need a minimum of $40$ units of protein and $28$ units of starch per day, what will be the minimum expenditure on food every day?

A quadrilateral that has consecutive sides of lengths $70$, $90$, $130$ and $110$ is inscribed in a circle and also has a circle inscribed in it. The point of tangency of the inscribed circle to the side of length $130$ divides that side into segments of lengths $x$ and $y$. If $y\ge x$, find $y-x$.

A solid has a square base of side $s$. The upper edge is parallel to the base and has length $2s$. All other edges have length $s$. What is the volume of the solid? [Note: the volume of the tetrahedron with all edges of length $\ell$ is $V=\frac{\sqrt{2}}{12}\ell^3$.]
Two circles of radii $3$ and $6$ touch internally. Find the area of the maximum rectangle outside the circle of radius $3$ and inside the circle of radius $6$.

In the figure, $AB=8$, $BC=7$ and $CA=6$. $\triangle PAB$ is similar to $\triangle PCA$. What is $PC$?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/bd_2007_p1_fig.png

In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle PAC=\angle PBC$. The perpendiculars from $P$ to $BC$ and $CA$ meet these lines at $L$ and $M$ respectively. $D$ is the midpoint of $AB$. What is the value of $\frac{DL}{DM}$?

We denote the greatest common divisor of integers $m$ and $n$ by $(m,n)$. For example, $(2,3)=1$ and $(10,15)=5$. Suppose $n(n+1)(n+2)$ is a square, where $n$ is an integer.

(a) What is $(n,n+1)$?

(b) What is $(n+1,n+2)$?

(c) What is $(n+1,n(n+2))$?

From your answers to (a), (b), (c), is it possible for $n(n+1)(n+2)$ to be a square?
If $x_1$, $x_2$ are the zeros of the polynomial $x^2-6x+1$, prove that for every nonnegative integer $n$, $x_1^n+x_2^n$ is an integer and is not divisible by $5$.
Writing down all the integers from $19$ to $92$ we make a large integer $N=192021\ldots 909192$. If $N$ is divisible by $3^k$, what is the maximum value of $k$?
Let $f(x)=x^6+x^5+\cdots+x+1$. Find the remainder when $f\left(x^7\right)$ is divided by $f(x)$.
Two parallel chords of a circle have lengths $10$ and $14$. The distance between them is $6$. The chord parallel to these chords and halfway between them has length $\sqrt{a}$. Find $a$.

A square has sides of length $2$. Let $S$ be the set of all line segments that have length $2$ and whose endpoints are on adjacent sides of the square. Let $L$ be the set of the midpoints of all segments in $S$. Find the area enclosed by $L$.
Find the area bounded by the curves $y=|x-1|$ and $x^2+y^2=2x$ (where $y\ge 0$).

Solve the inequality
$$2\cos x\le\left|\sqrt{1+\sin 2x}-\sqrt{1-\sin 2x}\right|.$$
Find the minima and maxima of $\left(\dfrac{\sin 10x}{\sin x}\right)^2$ in the interval $[0,\pi]$.

Sohag and Pias had some coconuts. They sold each coconut at a price equal to the total number of coconuts. Sohag and Pias began to take $20$ Taka each alternately from the money obtained. Sohag started the process. After a while he found that there was not enough money to take as before. Then he took the remaining money and, to make the sharing fair, he gave his pen to Pias. If they had taken $25$ Taka each alternately, the situation would have been almost the same, but in that case Sohag would have had to give his pencil to Pias. If the pen costs $5$ Taka more than the pencil, what is the price of the pencil? [The costs of the pen and the pencil are integers.]
Let $m+12=p^a$ and $m-12=p^b$, where $a$, $b$, $m$ are integers and $p$ is a prime number. Find all possible primes $p>0$. [Note: $p$ takes only three values.]
The sum of the first $2008$ odd positive integers is subtracted from the sum of the first $2008$ even positive integers. Find the result.

One coin is labeled with the number $1$, two different coins are labeled with the number $2$, three different coins are labeled with the number $3$, $\ldots$, $49$ different coins are labeled with the number $49$, and fifty different coins are labeled with the number $50$. All of these coins are then put into a black bag. The coins are then randomly drawn one by one. We need $10$ coins of any one type. What is the minimum number of coins that must be drawn to make sure that we have at least $10$ coins of one type?
Let $a$ be an integer. The number $m=4a+3$ is a multiple of $11$. What is the remainder when $a^4$ is divided by $11$? Show with proof.
The function $f(x)$ is a complicated nonlinear function. It satisfies $f(x)+f(1-x)=1$. Evaluate $\int_0^1 f(x)\,dx$.

Asmaa and her brother Ahmed are chess players. Asmaa's son Shamim and her daughter Sharmeen are also chess players. The worst player's twin (who is one of the $4$ chess players) and the best player are of opposite sex. The worst player and the best player are the same age. Who is the worst player?

The three digits $1,2,3$ are used to make a $5$-digit number. The five-digit number must contain at least one $1$, at least one $2$, and at least one $3$. How many such five-digit numbers can be made? (Hint: first count the number of words missing either a $1$ or a $2$ or a $3$.)

We want to find all integer solutions $(m,n)$ of $1+5\cdot 2^m=n^2$.

(a) Factor $n^2-1$;

(b) are $(n+1)$ and $(n-1)$ both even, or both odd, or is one even and the other odd?

(c) let $a=(n-1)/2$. Find an expression for $a(a+1)$;

(d) if $a$ is odd, is $a+1$ even or odd?

(e) from parts (c) and (d), is it possible for $a=1$, or $a(a+1)=\,$?

(f) find the only possible values $a$ can take and then find what $m$ and $n$ should be.

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral with $AB=BC=CD$ and $AC\ne BD$. Let $E$ be the intersection point of the diagonals of $ABCD$. $AE=DE$ if and only if $\angle BAD+\angle ADC=\vartheta$. Find $\vartheta$.

A quadrilateral $ABCD$ with $\angle BAD+\angle ADC>180^\circ$ circumscribes a circle with center $I$. A line through $I$ meets $AB$ and $CD$ at points $X$ and $Y$ respectively. If $IX=IY$, prove that $AX\cdot DY=BX\cdot CY$.
$300$ politicians are sitting in a room. Each one is corrupt or honest. At least one is honest. Given any two politicians, at least one is corrupt. How many are corrupt and how many are honest?

Find all integral solutions of the equation
$$\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{5}{y}=7.$$

Triangle $ABC$ is acute with the property that the bisector of $\angle BAC$, the altitude from $B$ to side $AC$ and the perpendicular bisector of $AB$ intersect at one point. Determine the angle $\angle BAC$.

Triangle $ABC$ is acute and $M$ is its circumcenter. Determine which points $P$ inside the triangle satisfy
$$1\le\frac{\angle APB}{\angle ACB}\le 2,\qquad 1\le\frac{\angle BPC}{\angle BAC}\le 2,\qquad 1\le\frac{\angle CPA}{\angle CBA}\le 2.$$

In triangle $ABC$, $\angle A=90^\circ$. $M$ is the midpoint of $BC$. Choose $D$ on $AC$ such that $AD=AM$. The circumcircles of triangles $AMC$ and $BDC$ intersect at $C$ and at a point $P$. What is the ratio of angles
$$\frac{\angle ACB}{\angle PCB}\,?$$

Forty MOVers (Mathematical Olympiad Volunteers) are sitting in a circle. Munir Hasan randomly chooses $3$ volunteers to help in the awards ceremony. In how many ways can the volunteers be chosen such that at least $2$ of the chosen volunteers were sitting next to each other before being chosen?

How many positive prime numbers can be written as an alternating sequence of $1$'s and $0$'s where the first and last digit is $1$? An alternating sequence of $1$'s and $0$'s is, for example, $N=1010101$, and has the property that $99N=99999999$.

The region $A$ is bounded by the $x$-axis, the line $y=\frac{x}{2}$, and the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{9}+y^2=1$. The region $B$ is bounded by the $y$-axis, the line $y=mx$, and the ellipse $\frac{x^2}{9}+y^2=1$. Find $m$ such that the area of region $A$ is equal to the area of region $B$.

Each square of an $n\times n$ chessboard is either red or green. The board is colored such that in any $2\times 2$ block of adjacent squares there are exactly $2$ green squares and $2$ red squares. How many ways can the chessboard be colored in this way? Note that the number of ways for a $2\times 2$ chessboard is $6$ and the number of ways for a $3\times 3$ chessboard is $14$, which is bigger than $2^3$.

$H$ is the orthocenter of acute triangle $ABC$. The triangle is inscribed in a circle with center $K$ and radius $R=1$. Let $D$ be the intersection of the lines $HK$ and $BC$. Also, $DK\cdot(DK-DH)=1$. Find the area of the region $ABHC$.

Find
$$S=\sum_{m=1}^{\infty}\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{m^2 n}{3^m\left(n3^m+m3^n\right)}.$$
Let $S=1^1+2^2+3^3+\cdots+2010^{2010}$. What is the remainder when $S$ is divided by $2$?

Isosceles triangle $ABC$ is right-angled at $B$ and $AB=3$. A circle of unit radius is drawn with its centre at one of the vertices of this triangle. Find the maximum value of the area of that part of the triangle that is not shared by the circle.

A sequence is formed in the following manner:

• $A(1)=1$;

• $A(n)$ = $f(m)$ digits $f(m)$ followed by $f(m)$ digits $0$,

where $m$ is the number of digits in $A(n-1)$ and $f(m)$ is the remainder when $m$ is divided by $9$. Find $A(30)$.

Given a point $P$ inside a circle $\Gamma$, two perpendicular chords through $P$ divide $\Gamma$ into distinct regions $a$, $b$, $c$, $d$, clockwise, such that $a$ contains the centre of $\Gamma$. Prove that $[a]+[c]\ge[b]+[d]$, where $[x]$ denotes the area of $x$.
How many regular polygons can be constructed from the vertices of a regular polygon with $2010$ sides? (Assume that the vertices of the $2010$-gon are indistinguishable.)

$a$ and $b$ are two positive integers, both less than $2010$, with $a\ne b$. Find the number of ordered pairs $(a,b)$ such that $a^2+b^2$ is divisible by $5$. Find $a+b$ such that $a^2+b^2$ is maximum.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with $AC>AB$. Let $P$ be the intersection point of the perpendicular bisector of $BC$ and the internal angle bisector of angle $CAB$. Let $X$ and $Y$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $P$ to the lines $AB$ and $AC$, respectively. Let $Z$ be the intersection point of the lines $XY$ and $BC$. Determine the value of $BZ/ZC$.
Find all prime numbers $p$ and integers $a$ and $b$ (not necessarily positive) such that $p^a+p^b$ is the square of a rational number.
Find the number of odd coefficients in the expansion of $(x+y)^{2010}$.

$a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k,\ldots,a_n$ is a sequence of distinct positive real numbers such that $a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_k$ and $a_k>a_{k+1}>\cdots>a_n$. A grasshopper is to jump along the real axis, starting at the point $O$ and making $n$ jumps to the right of lengths $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k,\ldots,a_n$ respectively. Prove that, once he reaches the rightmost point, he can come back to point $O$ by making $n$ jumps to the left of lengths $a_1,a_2,\ldots,a_k,\ldots,a_n$ in some order such that he never lands on a point which he already visited while jumping to the right. (The only exceptions are the point $O$ and the rightmost point.)

Prove that for any nonnegative integer $n$ the numbers $1,2,3,\ldots,4n$ can be divided into two mutually exclusive classes with an equal number of members so that the sums of the numbers in the two classes are equal.

In the first round of a chess tournament, each player plays against every other player exactly once. A player gets $3$, $1$ or $-1$ points respectively for winning, drawing or losing a match. After the end of the first round, it is found that the sum of the scores of all the players is $90$. How many players were there in the tournament?

$E$ is the midpoint of side $BC$ of rectangle $ABCD$. A point $X$ is chosen on $BE$. $DX$ meets the extension of $AB$ at $P$. Find, with proof, the position of $X$ for which the sum of the areas of $\triangle BPX$ and $\triangle DXC$ is maximum.
Let $A=2011!$ and $B=1006^{2011}$. Which one is larger? Show the logic.

Let $ABC$ be a scalene triangle with $\angle A=90^\circ$. The tangent line at $A$ to its circumcircle meets the line $BC$ at $M$, and the incircle touches $AC$ at $S$ and $AB$ at $R$. The lines $RS$ and $BC$ intersect at $N$ while the lines $AM$ and $SR$ intersect at $U$. Prove that the triangle $UMN$ is isosceles.
$p$ is a prime and the sum of the numbers from $1$ to $p$ is divisible by all primes less than or equal to $p$. Find the value of $p$ with proof.

Consider a group of $n>1$ people. Any two people of this group are related by mutual friendship or mutual enmity. Any friend of a friend and any enemy of an enemy is a friend. If $A$ and $B$ are friends/enemies then we count it as $1$ friendship/enmity. It is observed that the number of friendships and the number of enmities in the group are equal. Find all possible values of $n$.

$ABC$ is a right-angled triangle with $\angle A=90^\circ$, and $D$ is the midpoint of $BC$. A point $F$ is chosen on $AB$. $CA$ and $DF$ meet at $G$, and $GB\parallel AD$. $CF$ and $AD$ meet at $O$, and $AF=FO$. $GO$ meets $BC$ at $R$. Find the sides of $\triangle ABC$ if the area of $\triangle GDR$ is $2/\sqrt{15}$.
The repeat of a natural number is obtained by writing it twice in a row (for example, the repeat of $123$ is $123123$). Find a positive integer (if any) whose repeat is a perfect square.

Consider a square grid with $n$ rows and $n$ columns, where $n$ is odd (similar to a chessboard). Among the $n^2$ squares of the grid, $p$ are black and the others are white. The number of black squares is maximized while their arrangement is such that horizontally, vertically or diagonally neighboring black squares are separated by at least one white square between them. Show that there are infinitely many triplets of integers $(p,q,n)$ such that the number of white squares is $q^2$.

Subrata writes a letter to Ruponti every day (in successive intervals of $24$ hours) from Korea. But Ruponti receives the letters in intervals of $25$ hours. What is the number of the letter Ruponti receives on the $25$th day?

Superman is taking part in a hurdle race with $12$ hurdles. At any stage he can jump across any number of hurdles lying ahead. For example, he can cross all $12$ hurdles in one jump, or he can cross $7$ hurdles in the first jump, $1$ in the second and the rest in the third jump. In how many different ways can Superman complete the race?
In a given pentagon $ABCDE$, triangles $ABC$, $BCD$, $CDE$, $DEA$ and $EAB$ all have the same area. The lines $AC$ and $AD$ intersect $BE$ at points $M$ and $N$. Prove that $BM=EN$.

In triangle $ABC$, medians $AD$ and $CF$ intersect at point $G$. $P$ is an arbitrary point on $AC$. $PQ$ and $PR$ are parallel to $AD$ and $CF$ respectively. $PQ$ intersects $BC$ at $Q$ and $PR$ intersects $AB$ at $R$. If $QR$ intersects $AD$ at $M$ and $CF$ at $N$, prove that the area of triangle $GMN$ is $S/8$, where $S$ is the area enclosed by $PQ$, $PR$, $AD$, $CF$.
Show that for any prime $p$, there are either infinitely many or no positive integers $a$ such that $6p$ divides $a^p+1$. Find all those primes for which there exists no solution.

In an acute-angled triangle $ABC$, $\angle A=60^\circ$. Prove that the bisector of one of the angles formed by the altitudes drawn from $B$ and $C$ passes through the center of the circumcircle of the triangle $ABC$.

A decision-making problem will be resolved by tossing $2n+1$ coins. If heads come up in the majority, one option will be taken; for a majority of tails it will be the other one. Initially all the coins were fair. A witty mathematician replaced $n$ pairs of fair coins with $n$ pairs of biased coins, but in each pair the probability of obtaining heads with one coin is the same as the probability of obtaining tails with the other. Will this favour either of the options available? Justify with logic.
A triomino is an $L$-shaped pattern made from three unit squares. A $2^k\times 2^k$ chessboard has one of its squares missing. Show that the remaining board can be covered with triominoes.

A polygon is called degenerate if one of its vertices falls on the line that joins its two neighboring vertices. In a pentagon $ABCDE$, $AB=AE$ and $BC=DE$. $P$ and $Q$ are the midpoints of $AE$ and $AB$. $PQ\parallel CD$, and $BD$ is perpendicular to both $AB$ and $DE$. Prove that $ABCDE$ is a degenerate pentagon.

Let $g$ be a function from the set of ordered pairs of real numbers to the same set such that $g(x,y)=-g(y,x)$ for all real numbers $x$ and $y$. Find a real number $r$ such that $g(x,x)=r$ for all real numbers $x$.

Let $ABCDEF$ be a regular hexagon with $AB=7$. $M$ is the midpoint of $DE$. $AC$ and $BF$ intersect at $P$, $AC$ and $BM$ intersect at $Q$, $AM$ and $BF$ intersect at $R$. Find the value of $[APB]+[BQC]+[ARF]-[PQMR]$. Here $[X]$ denotes the area of polygon $X$.
If the fraction $a/b$ is greater than $31/17$ by the least amount while $b<17$, find $a/b$.

Let $x>1$ be an integer such that for any two positive integers $a$ and $b$, if $x$ divides $ab$ then $x$ divides $a$ or $x$ divides $b$. Find, with proof, the number of positive integers that divide $x$.

There are $n$ cities in a country. Between any two cities there is at most one road. Suppose that the total number of roads is $n$. Prove that there is a city such that starting from there it is possible to come back to it without ever travelling the same road twice.

If a prime number $p$ is such that $p+2q$ is prime for every positive integer $q$ smaller than $p$, then $p$ is called an awesome prime. Find the largest awesome prime and prove that it is indeed the largest such prime.

$ABC$ is an acute-angled triangle. The perpendiculars drawn from its vertices to the opposite sides are $AD$, $BE$ and $CF$. The line parallel to $DF$ through $E$ meets $BC$ at $Y$ and $BA$ at $X$. $DF$ and $CA$ meet at $Z$. The circumcircle of $XYZ$ meets $AC$ at $S$. Given $\angle B=33^\circ$, find the angle $\angle FSD$ with proof.

Six points $A,B,C,D,E,F$ are chosen on a circle anticlockwise. None of $AB$, $CD$, $EF$ is a diameter. Extended $AB$ and $DC$ meet at $Z$, $CD$ and $FE$ at $X$, $EF$ and $BA$ at $Y$. $AC$ and $BF$ meet at $P$, $CE$ and $BD$ at $Q$, and $AE$ and $DF$ at $R$. If $O$ is the point of intersection of $YQ$ and $ZR$, find the angle $\angle XOP$.

$X$ is a set of $n$ elements. $P_m(X)$ is the set of all $m$-element subsets (i.e. subsets that contain exactly $m$ elements) of $X$. Suppose $P_m(X)$ has $k$ elements. Prove that the elements of $P_m(X)$ can be ordered in a sequence $A_1,A_2,\ldots,A_i,\ldots,A_k$ that satisfies the two conditions:

(a) each element of $P_m(X)$ occurs exactly once in the sequence,

(b) for any $i$ such that $0<i<k$, the size of the set $A_i\cap A_{i+1}$ is $m-1$.

Rubai and Bidushi have some marbles. Bidushi told Rubai, "If you give me some marbles, I will return to you two more marbles than you gave me." Rubai said, "All right, I will first give you $6$ marbles." Then Rubai gave Bidushi $6$ marbles and Bidushi returned $8$ marbles to Rubai. Thus, after they have exchanged marbles $6$ times, Bidushi has no marbles left. How many marbles did Bidushi have in the beginning?

With his eyes closed, Towsif begins to place knights on a $21\times 23$ chessboard. After placing how many knights will Towsif be sure that on the next move at least one knight will attack another one? (In one move a knight goes straight for $2$ steps and the $3$rd step is at a right angle to the previous path.)

In $\triangle ABC$, $\angle B=90^\circ$. A circle is drawn taking $AB$ as a chord. $O$ is the center of the circle. $O$ and $C$ are not on the same side of $AB$. $BD$ is perpendicular to $AC$. Prove that $BD$ is a tangent to the circle if and only if $\angle BAO=\angle BAC$.

$97+98+\cdots+114+115=2014$. Here the sum of $19$ consecutive numbers is $2014$. Find the largest number of consecutive positive integers whose sum is exactly $2014$, and justify why this must be the largest number.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle with $\angle C=60^\circ$. Perpendiculars $AA_1$ and $BB_1$ are drawn from the points $A$ and $B$ to the sides $BC$ and $AC$ respectively. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $AB$. What is the value of $\dfrac{\angle A_1MB_1}{\angle A_1CB_1}$?

There are $n$ players in a chess tournament. Every player plays every other player exactly once, and there are no draws. Prove that the players can be labeled $1,2,\ldots,n$ so that $i$ beats $i+1$ for each $i\in\{1,2,3,\ldots,n-1\}$.

You are stuck in a 2D plane and your movement is limited to the two-dimensional grid shown below. You start at the point $(0,0)$ and have to reach the end point $(10,0)$. If your current position is $(x,y)$, you may move to $(x+1,y+1)$, $(x+1,y)$ and $(x+1,y-1)$ if the destination point is inside the grid. For example, you may move from $(0,0)$ to $(1,1)$, $(1,0)$ and $(1,-1)$; you may move from $(3,1)$ to $(4,1)$ and $(4,0)$. How many different paths exist from $(0,0)$ to $(10,0)$?

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/bd_2014_p8_fig.png

Suppose that you are at the leftmost bottom point of an $n\times n$ grid. You have to reach the rightmost topmost point. But the rule is that you can move only in the upward or rightward direction; you cannot move down or to the left. And as there are mines at the points along the diagonal, you cannot go to those places either. Determine how many ways there are to reach the destination.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/national-olympiads-bank/main/images/bd_2014_p9_fig.png
Consider $n\ge 2$ points in space. Prove that we can construct $n-1$ mutually parallel planes so that any two of the points are separated by a plane.

A crime is committed during the hartal. There are four witnesses. The witnesses are logicians and make the following statements:

• Witness One says exactly one of the four witnesses is a liar.

• Witness Two says exactly two of the four witnesses are liars.

• Witness Three says exactly three of the four witnesses are liars.

• Witness Four says exactly four of the four witnesses are liars.

Assume that each of these statements is either true or false. How many of the witnesses are liars?
Let $N$ be the number of pairs of integers $(m,n)$ that satisfy the equation $m^2+n^2=m^3$. Is $N$ finite or infinite? If $N$ is finite, what is its value?

Let $n$ be a positive integer. Consider the polynomial $p(x)=x^2+x+1$. What is $x^3 \pmod{p(x)}$, i.e. what is the remainder when $x^3$ is divided by $x^2+x+1$? For which positive integers $n$ is $x^{2n}+x^n+1$ divisible by $p(x)$?

There were $36$ participants at a BdMO event. Some of the participants shook hands with each other, but no two participants shook hands with each other more than once. Each participant recorded the number of handshakes they made. It was found that no two participants who made the same number of handshakes had shaken hands with each other. Find the maximum number of handshakes at the party. (When two participants shake hands with each other, this is counted as one handshake.)

A tetrahedron is a polyhedron composed of four triangular faces. Faces $ABC$ and $BCD$ of tetrahedron $ABCD$ meet at an angle of $\pi/6$. The area of triangle $ABC$ is $120$, the area of triangle $BCD$ is $80$, and $BC=10$. What is the volume of the tetrahedron? (The volume of a tetrahedron is one third of the area of its base times its height.)

Trapezoid $ABCD$ has sides $AB=92$, $BC=50$, $CD=19$, $AD=70$, with $AB$ parallel to $CD$. A circle with center $P$ on $AB$ is drawn tangent to $BC$ and $AD$. Given that $AP=m/n$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers, what is $m+n$?

In triangle $ABC$, the points $A'$, $B'$, $C'$ are on the sides $BC$, $AC$, $AB$ respectively, and $AA'$, $BB'$, $CC'$ are concurrent at the point $O$. Also,
$$\frac{AO}{OA'}+\frac{BO}{OB'}+\frac{CO}{OC'}=92.$$
Find the value of
$$\frac{AO}{OA'}\cdot\frac{BO}{OB'}\cdot\frac{CO}{OC'}.$$

(a) How many positive integer factors does $6000$ have?

(b) How many positive integer factors of $6000$ are not perfect squares?
$\triangle ABC$ is isosceles with $AB=AC$. $P$ is a point inside $\triangle ABC$ such that $\angle BCP=30^\circ$, $\angle APB=150^\circ$ and $\angle CAP=39^\circ$. Find $\angle BAP$.

Consider the set of integers $\{1,2,\ldots,100\}$. Let $\{x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{100}\}$ be some arbitrary arrangement of the integers $\{1,2,\ldots,100\}$, where all of the $x_i$ are different. Find the smallest possible value of the sum
$$S=|x_2-x_1|+|x_3-x_2|+\cdots+|x_{100}-x_{99}|+|x_1-x_{100}|.$$

Suppose there are $m$ Martians and $n$ Earthlings at an intergalactic peace conference. To ensure the Martians stay peaceful at the conference, we must make sure that no two Martians sit together, so that between any two Martians there is always at least one Earthling.

(a) Suppose all $m+n$ Martians and Earthlings are seated in a line. In how many ways can the Earthlings and Martians be seated in a line?

(b) Suppose now that the $m+n$ Martians and Earthlings are seated around a circular round table. In how many ways can the Earthlings and Martians be seated around the round table?

$\triangle ABC$ is an isosceles triangle with $AC=BC$ and $\angle ACB<60^\circ$. $I$ and $O$ are the incenter and circumcenter of $\triangle ABC$. The circumcircle of $\triangle BIO$ intersects $BC$ at $D\ne B$.

(a) Do the lines $AC$ and $DI$ intersect? Give a proof.

(b) What is the angle of intersection between the lines $OD$ and $IB$?

Aasma is a mathematician and devised an algorithm to find a husband. The strategy is:

• Start interviewing a maximum of $1000$ prospective husbands. Assign a ranking $r$ to each person that is a positive integer. No two prospects will have the same rank $r$.

• Reject the first $k$ men and let $H$ be the highest rank of these $k$ men.

• After rejecting the first $k$ men, select the next prospect with a rank greater than $H$ and then stop the search immediately. If no candidate is selected after $999$ interviews, the $1000$th person is selected.

Aasma wants to find the value of $k$ for which she has the highest probability of choosing the highest-ranking prospect among all $1000$ candidates without having to interview all $1000$ prospects.

(a) What is the probability that the highest-ranking prospect among all $1000$ prospects is the $(m+1)$th prospect?

(b) Assume the highest-ranking prospect is the $(m+1)$th person to be interviewed. What is the probability that the highest-ranked candidate among the first $m$ candidates is one of the first $k$ candidates who were rejected?

(c) What is the probability that the prospect with the highest rank is the $(m+1)$th person and that Aasma will choose the $(m+1)$th person using this algorithm?

(d) The total probability that Aasma will choose the highest-ranking prospect among the $1000$ prospects is the sum of the probabilities for each possible value of $m+1$, with $m+1$ ranging between $k+1$ and $1000$. Find the sum. To simplify your answer use the formula
$$\log N\approx\frac{1}{N-1}+\frac{1}{N-2}+\cdots+\frac{1}{2}+\frac{1}{1}.$$

(e) Find the value of $k$ that maximizes the probability of choosing the highest-ranking prospect without interviewing all $1000$ candidates. You may need to know that the maximum of the function $x\log\frac{A}{x-1}$ is approximately $(A+1)/e$, where $A$ is a constant and $e$ is Euler's number, $e=2.718\ldots$

$\triangle ABC$ is inscribed in circle $\omega$ with $AB=5$, $BC=7$, $AC=3$. The bisector of $\angle A$ meets side $BC$ at $D$ and circle $\omega$ at a second point $E$. Let $\gamma$ be the circle with diameter $DE$. Circles $\omega$ and $\gamma$ meet at $E$ and at a second point $F$. Then $AF^2=m/n$, where $m$ and $n$ are relatively prime positive integers. Find $m+n$.

The integral $Z(0)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\sqrt{\pi}$.

(a) Show that the integral $Z(j)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}e^{-x^2+jx}\,dx$, where $j$ is not a function of $x$, is
$$Z(j)=e^{\frac{j^2}{4}}Z(0).$$

(b) Show that
$$\frac{1}{Z(0)}\int x^{2n}e^{-x^2}\,dx=\frac{(2n-1)!!}{2^n},$$
where $(2n-1)!!$ is defined as $(2n-1)(2n-3)\times\cdots\times 3\times 1$.

(c) What is the number of ways to form $n$ pairs from $2n$ distinct objects? Interpret the previous part of the problem in terms of this answer.

Find the real solutions of the equation
$$x^2(2-x)^2=1+2(1-x)^2.$$
$AB$ is a diameter of a circle. Tangents $AD$ and $BC$ are drawn so that $AC$ and $BD$ intersect at a point on the circle. Suppose $AD=a$ and $BC=b$, with $a\ne b$. What is the diameter $AB$?

Urmi rolls four fair six-sided dice. She doesn't see the results. Her friend Ipshita tells her that the product of the numbers is $144$. Ipshita also says that the sum of the dice, $S$, satisfies $14\le S\le 18$. Urmi tells Ipshita that $S$ cannot be one of the numbers in the set $\{14,15,16,17,18\}$ if the product is $144$. Which number in the set $\{14,15,16,17,18\}$ is an impossible value for $S$?
Sabbir is counting the minimum number of lines $m$ that can be drawn in the plane so that they intersect in exactly $200$ distinct points. What is $m$?

Four circles are drawn with the sides of quadrilateral $ABCD$ as diameters. The two circles passing through $A$ meet again at $A'$. The two circles passing through $B$ meet again at $B'$. The two circles passing through $C$ meet again at $C'$. The two circles passing through $D$ meet again at $D'$. Suppose $A',B',C',D'$ are all distinct. Is the quadrilateral $A'B'C'D'$ similar to $ABCD$? Show with proof.

Find all pairs of integers $(m,n)$ satisfying
$$3\left(m^2+n^2\right)-7(m+n)=-4.$$

The vertices of a regular nonagon (9-sided polygon) are labeled with the digits $1$ through $9$ in such a way that the sum of the numbers on every three consecutive vertices is a multiple of $3$. Two acceptable arrangements are considered to be indistinguishable if one can be obtained from the other by rotating the nonagon in the plane. Find the number of distinguishable acceptable arrangements.

In a tournament of $n$ players, every pair of players plays exactly one match and there are no draws. A positive integer $k$ is called $n$-good if there exists a tournament of $n$ players in which for any $k$ players, there is at least one player other than these $k$ players who beats all of them.

(i) Prove that if $k$ is $n$-good then $n\ge 2^{k+1}-1$.

(ii) Find all $n$ such that $2$ is $n$-good.
Find all prime numbers whose square can be written as the sum of the cubes of two positive integers.

Prove that if $a,b,c$ are positive real numbers, then
$$\frac{a}{bc}+\frac{b}{ca}+\frac{c}{ab}\ge\frac{2}{a}+\frac{2}{b}-\frac{2}{c}.$$

Let $\alpha$ and $\omega$ be two circles such that $\omega$ goes through the center of $\alpha$. $\omega$ intersects $\alpha$ at $A$ and $B$. Let $P$ be any point on the circumference of $\omega$. The lines $PA$ and $PB$ intersect $\alpha$ again at $E$ and $F$ respectively. Prove that $AB=EF$.

$A$ is a positive real number and $n$ is a positive integer. Find the set of possible values of the infinite sum $x_0^n+x_1^n+x_2^n+\cdots$, where $x_0,x_1,x_2,\ldots$ are positive real numbers such that the infinite series $x_0+x_1+x_2+\cdots$ has sum $A$.

Prove that for every positive integer $n$ we can find a permutation of $1,2,\ldots,n$ such that the average of any two numbers does not appear between them. For example, $1,3,2,4$ works, but $1,4,2,3$ does not because $2$ is between $1$ and $3$.

When a function $f(x)$ is differentiated $n$ times, the function we get is denoted $f^n(x)$. If $f(x)=\frac{e^x}{x}$, find the value of
$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac{f^{2n}(1)}{(2n)!}.$$

Given three concentric circles $\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3$ with radii $r_1,r_2,r_3$ such that $r_1+r_3\ge 2r_2$, construct a line that intersects $\omega_1,\omega_2,\omega_3$ at $A,B,C$ respectively such that $AB=BC$.

The set of natural numbers $\mathbb{N}$ is partitioned into a finite number of subsets. Prove that there exists a subset $S$ such that for every natural number $n$, there are infinitely many multiples of $n$ in $S$.
Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. The internal angle bisectors of $\angle BAC$ and $\angle BDC$ meet at $P$, and $\angle APB=\angle CPD$. Prove that $AB+BD=AC+CD$.

Given a $2020\times 2020$ chessboard, what is the maximum number of warriors you can put on its cells such that no two warriors attack each other? A warrior is a special chess piece which can move either $3$ steps forward and $1$ step sideways, or $2$ steps forward and $2$ steps sideways, in any direction.

Lazim rolls two $24$-sided dice. From the two rolls, Lazim selects the die with the higher number. $N$ is an integer not greater than $24$. What is the largest possible value of $N$ such that there is a more than $50\%$ chance that the die Lazim selects is larger than or equal to $N$?
How many integers $n$ are there with $1\le n\le 2020$ such that $n^n$ is a perfect square?

Let $R$ be the set of all rectangles centered at the origin and with perimeter $1$ (the center of a rectangle is the intersection point of its two diagonals). Let $S$ be a region that contains all of the rectangles in $R$ (region $A$ contains region $B$ if $B$ is completely inside $A$). The minimum possible area of $S$ has the form $\pi a$, where $a$ is a real number. Find $1/a$.
$56$ lines are drawn in a plane such that no three of them are concurrent. If the lines intersect at exactly $594$ points, what is the maximum number of them that could have the same slope?

In triangle $ABC$, $AB=52$, $BC=34$ and $CA=50$. We split $BC$ into $n$ equal segments by placing $n-1$ new points. Among these points are the feet of the altitude, the median and the angle bisector from $A$. What is the smallest possible value of $n$?
$f$ is a one-to-one function from the set of positive integers to itself such that $f(xy)=f(x)f(y)$. Find the minimum possible value of $f(2020)$.

$f$ is a function on the set of complex numbers such that $f(z)=1/(z^*)$, where $z^*$ is the complex conjugate of $z$. $S$ is the set of complex numbers $z$ such that the real part of $f(z)$ lies between $1/2020$ and $1/2018$. If $S$ is treated as a subset of the complex plane, the area of $S$ can be expressed as $m\pi$, where $m$ is an integer. What is $m$?

(Note: the complex plane is just like the Cartesian plane, where the $x$-axis is renamed the real axis and the $y$-axis is renamed the imaginary axis.) Remember, a complex number is a number of the form $a+bi$, where $a$ and $b$ are real numbers and $i$ is a number such that $i^2=-1$. If $z=a+bi$, the complex conjugate of $z$ is $z^*=a-bi$.

We call a permutation of the numbers $1,2,3,\ldots,n$ kawaii if there is exactly one number that is greater than its position. For example, $1,4,3,2$ is a kawaii permutation (when $n=4$) because only the number $4$ is greater than its position $2$. How many kawaii permutations are there if $n=14$?

Let $ABCD$ be a convex quadrilateral. $O$ is the intersection of $AC$ and $BD$, with $AO=3$, $BO=4$, $CO=5$, $DO=6$. $X$ and $Y$ are points on the segments $AB$ and $CD$ respectively, such that $X$, $O$, $Y$ are collinear. The minimum of $XB/XA+YC/YD$ can be written as $\frac{a\sqrt{c}}{b}$, where $a/b$ is in lowest terms and $c$ is not divisible by any square number greater than $1$. What is the value of $10a+b+c$?

Bristy wants to build a special set $A$. She starts with $A=\{0,42\}$. At any step, she can add an integer $x$ to the set $A$ if it is a root of a polynomial which uses the already existing integers in $A$ as coefficients. She keeps doing this, adding more and more numbers to $A$. After she eventually runs out of numbers to add to $A$, how many numbers will be in $A$?

$ABCD$ is a convex quadrilateral where $BC=CD$, $AC=AD$, $\angle BCD=96^\circ$ and $\angle ACD=69^\circ$. Set $P_0=A$ and $Q_0=B$. We inductively define $P_{n+1}$ to be the center of the incircle of $CDP_n$, and $Q_{n+1}$ to be the center of the incircle of $CDQ_n$. If $\angle Q_{2024}Q_{2025}P_{2025}-90^\circ=\frac{2k-1}{2^n}$, compute $k+n$.
For a positive integer $n$, let $A(n)$ be equal to the remainder when $n$ is divided by $11$, and let $T(n)=A(1)+A(2)+\cdots+A(n)$. Find the value of $A(T(2021))$.

Let $u$ and $v$ be real numbers. The minimum value of
$$\sqrt{u^2+v^2}+\sqrt{(u-1)^2+v^2}+\sqrt{u^2+(v-1)^2}+\sqrt{(u-1)^2+(v-1)^2}$$
can be written as $\sqrt{n}$. Find the value of $10n$.

Let $\triangle ABC$ be a triangle with incenter $I$. Points $E$ and $F$ are on the segments $AC$ and $BC$ respectively such that $AE=AI$ and $BF=BI$. If $EF$ is the perpendicular bisector of $CI$, then $\angle ACB$ in degrees can be written as $m/n$, where $m$ and $n$ are coprime positive integers. Find the value of $m+n$.
$P(x)$ is a polynomial in $x$ with non-negative integer coefficients. If $P(1)=5$ and $P(P(1))=177$, what is the sum of all possible values of $P(10)$?

In how many ways can you roll three $20$-sided dice such that the sum of the three rolls is exactly $42$? Here the order of the rolls matters.

(Note that a $20$-sided die is very much like a regular six-sided die other than the fact that it has $20$ faces instead of the regular six.)

Let $\triangle ABC$ be an acute-angled triangle. The external bisector of $\angle BAC$ meets the line $BC$ at the point $N$. Let $M$ be the midpoint of $BC$. $P$ and $Q$ are two points on the line $AN$ such that $\angle PMN=\angle MQN=90^\circ$. If $PN=5$ and $BC=3$, then the length of $QA$ can be expressed as $a/b$, where $a$ and $b$ are coprime positive integers. What is the value of $a+b$?

A binary string is a word containing only $0$s and $1$s. In a binary string, a $1$-run is a non-extendable substring containing only $1$s. Given a positive integer $n$, let $B(n)$ be the number of $1$-runs in the binary representation of $n$. For example, $B(107)=3$, since $107$ in binary is $1101011$, which has exactly three $1$-runs. What is the following expression equal to?
$$B(1)+B(2)+B(3)+\cdots+B(255)$$

Shakur and Tiham are playing a game. Initially, Shakur picks a positive integer not greater than $1000$. Then Tiham picks a positive integer strictly smaller than that. Then they keep on doing this, taking turns to pick progressively smaller positive integers until someone picks $1$. After that, all the numbers that have been picked so far are added up. The person picking the number $1$ wins if and only if this sum is a perfect square. Otherwise, the other player wins. What is the sum of all possible values of $n$ such that if Shakur starts with the number $n$, he has a winning strategy?

A positive integer $n$ is called nice if it has at least $3$ proper divisors and it is equal to the sum of its three largest proper divisors. For example, $6$ is nice because its largest proper divisors are $3,2,1$ and $6=3+2+1$. Find the number of nice integers not greater than $3000$.

$A_1A_2A_3A_4A_5A_6A_7A_8$ is a regular octagon. Let $P$ be a point inside the octagon such that the distances from $P$ to $A_1A_2$, $A_2A_3$ and $A_3A_4$ are $24$, $26$ and $27$ respectively. The length of $A_1A_2$ can be written as $a\sqrt{b}-c$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive integers and $b$ is not divisible by any square number other than $1$. What is the value of $a+b+c$?

How many quadruples of positive integers $(a,b,m,n)$ are there such that all of the following statements hold?

(1) $a,b<5000$

(2) $m,n<22$

(3) $\gcd(m,n)=1$

(4) $\left(a^2+b^2\right)^m=(ab)^n$

A function $g:\mathbb{Z}\to\mathbb{Z}$ is called adjective if $g(m)+g(n)>\max\left(m^2,n^2\right)$ for every pair of integers $m$ and $n$. Let $f$ be an adjective function such that the value of
$$f(1)+f(2)+\cdots+f(30)$$
is minimized. Find the smallest possible value of $f(25)$.
Find all non-negative integer solutions $(x,y,z)$ of the equation $$x!+2^y=z!$$ (Here $x!=x\cdot(x-1)!$ and $0!=1$; for example, $5!=5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1=120$.)

Let $\{a_1, a_2,\ldots,a_n\}$ be a set of $n$ real numbers whose sum equals $S$. It is known that each number in the set is less than $\frac{S}{n-1}$. Prove that for any three numbers $a_i$, $a_j$ and $a_k$ of the set, $a_i+a_j>a_k$.

For any positive integer $n$, define $f(n)$ to be the smallest positive integer that does not divide $n$; for example, $f(1)=2$ and $f(6)=4$. Prove that for any positive integer $n$, either $f(f(n))$ or $f(f(f(n)))$ is equal to $2$.

Let $ABCD$ be an isosceles trapezium inscribed in a circle $\omega$, with $AB\parallel CD$. Let $P$ be a point on the circle $\omega$, and let $H_1$ and $H_2$ be the orthocenters of triangles $PAD$ and $PBC$ respectively. Prove that the length of $H_1H_2$ remains constant as $P$ varies on the circle.
Consider an integrable function $f:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ such that $af(a)+bf(b)=0$ whenever $ab=1$. Find the value of the integral $$\int_{0}^{\infty} f(x) \,dx.$$

We are given $n$ intervals $[l_1,r_1],[l_2,r_2],\ldots, [l_n,r_n]$ on the number line, which can be divided into two sets such that no two intervals in the same set overlap. Prove that there are at most $n-1$ pairs of overlapping intervals.

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle and $\omega$ its circumcircle. The perpendicular from $A$ to $BC$ intersects $BC$ at $D$ and $\omega$ again at $K$. The circle through $A$ and $D$ tangent to $BC$ at $D$ intersects $\omega$ again at $E$. The line $AE$ intersects $BC$ at $T$, and $TK$ intersects $\omega$ again at $S$. Let $SD$ intersect $\omega$ again at $X$. Prove that $X$ is the reflection of $A$ in the perpendicular bisector of $BC$.

Joy has an $n \times n$ board. At every step, he colours a cell of the board; he cannot colour any cell more than once. He also counts points while colouring: at first he has $0$ points, and at every step, after colouring a cell $c$, he takes the largest possible set $S$ of cells forming a "$+$" sign whose cells are all coloured and whose centre is $c$, and he gets $|S|$ points. After colouring the whole $n \times n$ board, what is the maximum possible number of points he can have?

Let $ABC$ be an acute triangle, and let $D$ be the point on side $BC$ such that $AD$ bisects the angle $\angle BAC$. A line $l$ is tangent to the circumcircles of triangles $ADB$ and $ADC$ at the points $K$ and $L$, respectively. Let $M$, $N$ and $P$ be the midpoints of $BD$, $DC$ and $KL$, respectively. Prove that $l$ is tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $MNP$.

Consider all polynomials of degree $2023$ $$P(x)=x^{2023}+a_1x^{2022}+a_2x^{2021}+\cdots+a_{2022}x+a_{2023}$$ with real coefficients such that $P(0)+P(1)=0$ and $P$ has $2023$ real roots $r_1, r_2,\ldots, r_{2023}$ (not necessarily distinct) with $0\leq r_i\leq1$ for all $i$. What is the maximum value of $r_1 r_2 \cdots r_{2023}$?
Find all prime numbers $p$ and $q$ such that $$p^3-3^q=10.$$

Let $ABCD$ be a square. Points $E$ and $F$ lie on the sides $AB$ and $BC$, respectively, such that $BE = BF$. The line through $B$ perpendicular to $CE$ intersects $CE$ and $AD$ at the points $G$ and $H$, respectively. The lines $FH$ and $CE$ intersect at the point $P$, and the lines $GF$ and $CD$ intersect at the point $Q$. Prove that the line $DP$ is perpendicular to the line $BQ$.

Let $a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{2024}$ be a permutation of $1, 2, \ldots, 2024$. Find the minimum possible value of $$\sum_{i=1} ^{2023} \left[(a_i+a_{i+1})\left(\frac{1}{a_i}+\frac{1}{a_{i+1}}\right)+\frac{1}{a_ia_{i+1}}\right].$$

Let $I$ be the incenter of triangle $ABC$ and $P$ a point such that $PI$ is perpendicular to $BC$ and $PA$ is parallel to $BC$. The line parallel to $BC$ which is tangent to the incircle of triangle $ABC$ (other than $BC$) intersects $AB$ and $AC$ at the points $Q$ and $R$ respectively. Prove that $\angle BPQ = \angle CPR$.
Find all polynomials $P(x)$ for which there exists a sequence $a_1, a_2, a_3, \ldots$ of real numbers such that $$a_m + a_n = P(mn)$$ for all positive integers $m$ and $n$.
Find all functions $f:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{N}$ such that $$f\left(\left\lceil \frac{f(m)}{n} \right\rceil\right)=\left\lceil \frac{m}{f(n)} \right\rceil$$ for all $m,n \in \mathbb{N}$.
Let $k$ be a positive integer. Show that there exist infinitely many positive integers $n$ such that $\frac{n^n-1}{n-1}$ has at least $k$ distinct prime divisors.

Let $ABC$ be a triangle and $M$ the midpoint of the side $BC$. The perpendicular bisector of $BC$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$ at the points $K$ and $L$, where $K$ and $A$ lie on opposite sides of $BC$. A circle passing through $L$ and $M$ intersects $AK$ at the points $P$ and $Q$, with $P$ on the segment $AQ$. The line $LQ$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $KMQ$ again at $R$. Prove that $BPCR$ is a cyclic quadrilateral.

Juty and Azgor play the following game on a $(2n+1) \times (2n+1)$ board, with Juty moving first. Initially all cells are white. On Juty's turn, she colours a white cell green, and on Azgor's turn, he colours a white cell red. The game ends when all cells of the board are coloured. Juty wins if all the green cells are connected, i.e. any two green cells are joined by a chain of green cells in which consecutive cells are neighbours (two cells are neighbours if they share at least one corner); otherwise Azgor wins. Determine which player has a winning strategy.

One day a room contained several inhabitants of an island where only truth-tellers and liars live. Three of them made the following statements:
• "There are no more than three of us here. We are all liars."
• "There are no more than four of us here. Not all of us are liars."
• "There are five of us here. At least three of us are liars."
How many people are in the room, and how many of them are liars?

Let $ABC$ be a triangle with circumcenter $O$ and orthocenter $H$. Let $D, E$ and $F$ be the feet of the perpendiculars from $A, B$ and $C$ to the opposite sides, respectively, and let $A'$ be the reflection of $A$ in the line $EF$. Prove that $HOA'D$ is a cyclic quadrilateral.

Two players play on a $100 \times 100$ grid. Initially the whole board is black. On his move, $A$ selects a $4 \times 4$ subgrid and colours it white; on his move, $B$ selects a $3 \times 3$ subgrid and colours it black. $A$ wants to make the whole board white. Can he do it?
Find all prime numbers $p, q$ such that $$p(p+1)(p^2+1) = q^2(q^2+q+1) + 2025.$$

Let the incircle of triangle $ABC$, with center $I$, touch the sides $BC, CA$ and $AB$ at the points $D, E$ and $F$ respectively. Let $P$ be the foot of the perpendicular from $I$ to the line $AD$, and let $M$ be the midpoint of $DE$. If $N$ is the intersection point of $PM$ and $AC$, prove that $DN \parallel EF$.

Yamin and Tamim play a game with subsets of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$, where $n \geq 3$.
• Tamim starts the game with the empty set.
• On Yamin's turn, he adds a proper non-empty subset of $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$ to his collection $F$ of blocked sets.
• On Tamim's turn, he adds to his set, or removes from it, one positive integer at most $n$; however, he can never make a move after which his set is one of the blocked sets in $F$.
Tamim wins if he can make his set equal to $\{1, 2, \ldots, n\}$; Yamin wins if he can prevent this. Yamin goes first and they alternate moves. Does Tamim have a winning strategy?
Find all functions $f: \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ such that $$f(xf(y)-y) + f(xy-x) + f(x+y) = 2xy$$ for all $x, y \in \mathbb{R}$.

In triangle $ABC$, $DB$ and $DC$ are tangent to the circumcircle of triangle $ABC$. Let $B'$ be the reflection of $B$ in the line $AC$, and similarly let $C'$ be the reflection of $C$ in the line $AB$. If the line $BC$ intersects the circumcircle of triangle $DB'C'$ at $E$ and $F$, prove that $AE = AF$.
If $\frac{b}{a}=5$ and $\frac{c}{b}=7$, find the value of $\frac{a+b}{b+c}$.
Let $f$ be a continuous function satisfying $f(1+x)=f(1-x)$ for every real $x$. It is given that the equation $f(x)=0$ has exactly $2026$ distinct roots. Find the sum of all the roots.
$ABCD$ is a cyclic quadrilateral, and $F$ is the midpoint of the arc $AB$ not containing $C$ or $D$. Let $P = CF \cap BD$ and $Q = DF \cap AC$. Prove that $PQ \parallel AB$.

Let $S = \{1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7\}$. Mr. Teham chooses a pair of elements of $S$ and writes down the greater number of the pair; for example, if he chooses $\{6, 7\}$ he writes $7$. Find the sum of all the numbers he has written after choosing every possible pair exactly once.

Triangle $ABC$ is isosceles with $\angle ACB = 90^\circ$. Points $E$ and $F$ are two distinct points on the arc $AB$ of its circumcircle not containing $C$. Let $D = CE \cap AB$ and $G = CF \cap AB$.
(1) Prove that $CE \cdot DG = k \cdot EF \cdot CG$ for some real number $k$ not depending on the points $E$ and $F$.
(2) Find the value of $k$.
Prove that for every positive integer $n$ $$I_n = \int_{0}^{1} x^{n}\sqrt{1-x}\,dx = \frac{2^{2n+2}\,n!\,(n+1)!}{(2n+3)!}.$$
Find all positive integers $n$ of the form $n = p^k$, where $p$ is a prime number and $k$ is a positive integer, such that $$n = x^3 - 2x^2 + 2x - 1$$ for some integer $x$.
Find all triples $(k, m, n)$, where $k$ is a prime number and $m, n$ are non-negative integers, such that $$k^m - n^3 - 1 = 26.$$

Let $\{a_1, a_2, \ldots, a_{1013}\}$ and $\{b_1, b_2, \ldots, b_{1013}\}$ be two disjoint subsets of $\{1, 2, 3, \ldots, 2026\}$ such that $|a_i - b_i| \equiv 1 \pmod{5}$ for all $1\le i\le 1013$, and let $$S = \sum_{i=1}^{1013} |a_i - b_i|.$$
(1) Prove that $S \equiv 3 \pmod{5}$.
(2) Prove that $S \equiv 1 \pmod{2}$.
(3) Prove that the last decimal digit of $S$ is $3$.

There are $n$ people in a math camp. Each person has exactly $8$ acquaintances in the camp. If two people are acquainted with each other, then exactly $4$ other people are acquainted with both of them; if two people are not acquainted with each other, then exactly $2$ other people are acquainted with both of them. Find all possible values of $n$.
